docs.title: corm
docs.text: corm wraps nested dictionaries from parsed JSON or YAML in lightweight Python entities. If you've ever needed to get the parent of a nested model, corm gives the child a back-reference to its parent. It also resolves ID references through an in-memory identity map. corm wraps the input dictionaries in place without copying or validating them. Undeclared keys are preserved, and dict() exports the data as dictionaries again.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A project API returns users and sprints. Each sprint embeds its tasks, and each task stores an assignee_id. The example follows both links, moves a task to a new sprint, and checks that the export preserves the task's assignee and undeclared keys such as labels.

Download the runnable project example.

from corm import Entity, Field, KeyNested, Nested, Relationship, Storage


class User(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)
    name: str
    tasks: list["Task"] = Relationship()


class Task(Entity):
    title: str
    assignee: User = KeyNested(User.id, origin="assignee_id", back_populates="tasks")
    sprint: "Sprint | None" = Relationship()


class Sprint(Entity):
    name: str
    tasks: list[Task] = Nested(back_populates="sprint")


class Project(Entity):
    name: str
    users: list[User] = Nested()
    sprints: list[Sprint] = Nested()


payload = {
    "name": "Customer portal",
    "archived": False,
    "users": [{"id": 42, "name": "Amina", "timezone": "UTC"}],
    "sprints": [
        {
            "name": "Sprint 12",
            "tasks": [
                {
                    "title": "Add invoice download",
                    "assignee_id": 42,
                    "labels": ["billing"],
                }
            ],
        },
        {"name": "Sprint 13", "tasks": []},
    ],
}

project = Project(payload, Storage())
current_sprint, next_sprint = project.sprints
(task,) = current_sprint.tasks
(user,) = project.users

assert project.name == "Customer portal"
assert task.title == "Add invoice download"
assert task.sprint is current_sprint
assert task.assignee is user
assert user.tasks == [task]

task.sprint = next_sprint

assert current_sprint.tasks == []
assert next_sprint.tasks == [task]
assert task.sprint is next_sprint
assert task.assignee is user
assert user.tasks == [task]

assert project.dict() == {
    "name": "Customer portal",
    "archived": False,
    "users": [{"id": 42, "name": "Amina", "timezone": "UTC"}],
    "sprints": [
        {"name": "Sprint 12", "tasks": []},
        {
            "name": "Sprint 13",
            "tasks": [
                {
                    "title": "Add invoice download",
                    "assignee_id": 42,
                    "labels": ["billing"],
                }
            ],
        },
    ],
}

docs.title: When to use corm
docs.text:
Use corm to edit a document in memory when your code often navigates from a child to its parent or follows references by ID. corm is not a validation library and is not optimized for speed. Choose a validation or decoding library for untrusted input, a dot-access wrapper for simple attribute access, or SQLite with an ORM when you need queries, joins, or transactions.

Tool Validation Back-references References by ID Preserves unknown keys Typed attribute access corm No Built in with back_populates Built in with KeyNested Yes, by default Yes, for declared fields Pydantic Yes Application code Application code With extra="allow" Yes attrs + cattrs / msgspec attrs validators / typed decoding in msgspec Application code Application code Requires explicit handling Yes python-box No Application code Application code Yes, as mapping keys Dynamic dot access In-memory SQLite + ORM Database constraints With mapped relationships With foreign keys and joins Explicit storage, such as a JSON column With typed ORM models

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install with pip install corm. corm is in early development, and its API may change.

See the entity guide to define your own entities, or read the changelog for recent changes.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to corm are documented here. The format follows Keep a Changelog.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Pair a Nested or KeyNested field with a reverse Relationship using back_populates. Editing either side updates both fields. (#33)
  • Infer the related entity type and whether it is a list from annotations. (#32)
  • Ship a py.typed marker and expose a CormError hierarchy for library errors. (#34)
  • Automate PyPI publishing and GitHub Releases from version tags. (#29)

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Require Python 3.11 or newer and test on Python 3.11 through 3.15. Use uv, Ruff, and pre-commit for development. (#28)
  • Expose AccessMode as a combinable IntFlag. (#34)

docs.title: Deprecated
docs.text: • Use back_populates for new reverse links. The back_relation argument remains available and emits a deprecation warning. (#33)

docs.title: Removed
docs.text: • Remove the unused corm.hooks module. (#27)

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Preserve nested entity data when exporting dictionaries. Fix field inference and relationship reassignment, and reject duplicate keys before loading relationships for the duplicate entity. (#27)
  • Resolve relationships to instances of subclasses of the declared type. (#30)
  • Keep primary-key lookup in sync with key changes and keep relation reads from changing the index. Index relation membership while preserving order. (#31)

docs.title: Is corm fast or memory-efficient?
docs.text:
corm is designed for convenient navigation and editing of related data in memory. It is not optimized for speed. The storage keeps references to the entities it indexes and the entities in its relation index.

The benchmark measures setup and relationship traversal for dictionaries and corm entities.

docs.title: Does corm validate input?
docs.text: corm uses annotations for typed attribute access and relation inference. It checks that required fields are present and that it can maintain declared relationships and keys. It does not validate field value types or coerce data.

docs.title: How is this different from Pydantic?
docs.text: Pydantic validates and parses input into typed models. If you want a nested child to know its parent in Pydantic, you set up that link in application code. corm gives the child a parent link through a paired Nested and Relationship and resolves references by ID through Storage. It works directly with the input dictionary and preserves undeclared keys by default.

docs.title: Can I use it with Pydantic or attrs models?
docs.text: Yes. Validate or structure your input first, then pass a dictionary from model_dump() or attrs.asdict() into corm. Use output keys that match your corm fields' origin settings. You can also pass entity.dict() back to your validation or structuring layer. corm wraps the dictionaries you pass in, so edits through corm update those dictionaries.

docs.title: Open feature requests
docs.text:
• Query API
  • Exclude fields during entity creation
  • Exclude fields during dictionary export
  • Entity namespaces, a storage context, and moving entities between storages

docs.title: Entities
docs.text: An Entity wraps a dictionary. Declare the fields you want to access as attributes, then pass the dictionary and a Storage to the entity constructor. Attribute writes update the wrapped dictionary. Undeclared keys stay in the data and are included in entity.dict().

docs.title: Field declarations
docs.text: An explicit Field or relation descriptor becomes a field. A public annotation such as name: str declares a field, and a public class value such as description = "Project member" supplies a default. Unannotated methods, properties, other callables, and names starting with _ stay out of the implicit field declarations. Annotations describe field types for editors and type checkers. corm uses relation annotations to infer related entity types and whether a field holds one entity or a list.

docs.title: Input and output keys
docs.text: origin is the dictionary key a field reads and writes. It defaults to the attribute name. destination is the key used by dict() and defaults to origin. When they differ, the export uses the destination key in place of the origin. Load the export with a model that expects the destination key, or map it back before reloading with the same model.

docs.title: Access and export
docs.text:
Field and Nested default to AccessMode.ALL. Combine AccessMode flags with |. LOAD processes the field at construction, SET permits assignment, and DUMP exports the field through its declared destination. The GET flag describes a readable field. The current descriptors still allow direct reads without it. KeyNested defaults to GET_SET_LOAD so the original key stays in the exported data. A reverse Relationship lives in the relation index.

dict(strip_none=True) omits declared fields with DUMP whose value is None, including fields in declared nested entities. Undeclared keys with None values are preserved.

The example reads an ID from user_id, exports it as id, and uses a read-only display name. It also shows an optional field and an undeclared key.

from corm import AccessMode, Entity, Field, ReadOnlyFieldError, Storage


class User(Entity):
    id: int = Field(origin="user_id", destination="id")
    name: str = Field(mode=AccessMode.GET | AccessMode.LOAD | AccessMode.DUMP)
    description: str = "Project member"
    nickname: str | None = Field(default=None)


payload = {"user_id": 33, "name": "Amina", "timezone": "UTC", "metadata": None}
user = User(payload, Storage())

assert user.id == 33
user.id = 34
assert payload["user_id"] == 34
assert user.name == "Amina"

try:
    user.name = "Mina"
except ReadOnlyFieldError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("The name field is read-only")

assert user.dict() == {
    "id": 34,
    "name": "Amina",
    "description": "Project member",
    "nickname": None,
    "timezone": "UTC",
    "metadata": None,
}
assert user.dict(strip_none=True) == {
    "id": 34,
    "name": "Amina",
    "description": "Project member",
    "timezone": "UTC",
    "metadata": None,
}

docs.title: Default values
docs.text:
Supply a plain class value or pass default= to Field, Nested, or KeyNested. corm calls a default factory for each instance whose input lacks that field. An explicit None value in the input counts as a supplied value.

from corm import Entity, Field, Storage


class Foo(Entity):
    inplace = 1
    in_field = Field(default=2)
    in_field_callable = Field(default=list)


storage = Storage()
foo = Foo(data={}, storage=storage)

assert foo.inplace == 1
assert foo.in_field == 2
assert foo.in_field_callable == []

A callable assigned directly to the class remains a class attribute. Use Field(default=list) if you want corm to call list as a field's default factory.

from corm import Entity, Storage


class Foo(Entity):
    inplace = list


storage = Storage()
foo = Foo(data={}, storage=storage)

assert foo.inplace is list  # still callable, not new empty list

docs.title: Key relationships
docs.text: KeyNested takes the related entity's primary-key field as its related_entity_field argument. It infers many=True from list annotations such as list[Address] or list["Address"]. You can still pass many= to set this explicitly.

docs.title: Resolve a list of keys
docs.text:
Use origin when the input key name differs from the attribute name. This example reads the entity_ids list and resolves each ID to a stored entity. Access the resulting list through holder.entities.

from corm import Entity, Field, KeyNested, Storage


class SomeEntity(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)
    name: str


class EntityHolder(Entity):
    name: str
    entities: list[SomeEntity] = KeyNested(
        related_entity_field=SomeEntity.id,
        origin="entity_ids",
    )


storage = Storage()
entity = SomeEntity({"id": 123, "name": "entity"}, storage=storage)
holder = EntityHolder({"entity_ids": [123], "name": "holder"}, storage=storage)

assert holder.entities == [entity]

docs.title: Bidirectional key relationships
docs.text:
Set back_populates on KeyNested to name the Relationship on the entity referenced by the key. The reverse field's annotation or many= setting controls whether it returns a single owner or a list of owners. An owner can be loaded before the related entity. Its reverse link is available when that key appears in storage.

If the target inherits its primary-key field, annotate the KeyNested attribute with the target subclass to select its Relationship.

from corm import (
    Entity,
    Field,
    KeyNested,
    Relationship,
    Storage,
)


class SomeEntity(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)
    name: str
    holder: "EntityHolder | None" = Relationship()


class EntityHolder(Entity):
    name: str
    entity: SomeEntity = KeyNested(
        related_entity_field=SomeEntity.id,
        origin="entity_id",
        back_populates="holder",
    )


storage = Storage()
holder = EntityHolder({"name": "holder", "entity_id": 123}, storage=storage)
entity = SomeEntity({"id": 123, "name": "entity"}, storage=storage)

assert holder.entity == entity
assert entity.holder == holder

docs.title: Change relationships between entities
docs.text:
Writing through either field updates the owner's stored key. Assign an owner to a single Relationship to move the link, or assign None to clear it. For a reverse list, append or remove owners or assign the replacement list. If the owning KeyNested field is a list, the operation adds or removes the corresponding key. With required=False, edits to the list of resolved entities preserve keys that are still missing. Assigning a replacement list directly to the owning field replaces its stored keys.

from corm import Entity, Field, KeyNested, Relationship, Storage


class SomeEntity(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)
    name: str
    holder: "EntityHolder | None" = Relationship()


class EntityHolder(Entity):
    entity: SomeEntity | None = KeyNested(
        related_entity_field=SomeEntity.id,
        origin="entity_id",
        back_populates="holder",
    )


storage = Storage()
entity1 = SomeEntity({"id": 123, "name": "entity1"}, storage=storage)
entity2 = SomeEntity({"id": 321, "name": "entity2"}, storage=storage)
holder = EntityHolder(
    data={"entity_id": 123},
    storage=storage,
)

holder.entity = entity2

assert entity1.holder is None
assert entity2.holder is holder
assert holder.entity is entity2
assert holder.dict() == {"entity_id": 321}

new_holder = EntityHolder({"entity_id": None}, storage)
entity2.holder = new_holder

assert holder.entity is None
assert holder.dict() == {"entity_id": None}
assert new_holder.entity is entity2
assert new_holder.dict() == {"entity_id": 321}

docs.title: Keys stored as objects
docs.text:
Pass a KeyManager when a reference is stored in a shape other than a bare key. Implement get(data) to extract the hashable key used by Storage and prepare_to_set(entity) to produce the stored representation when assigning an entity. A list relation calls these methods for each reference. Return None from prepare_to_set(None) for a cleared single reference.

This example reads and writes team member references stored as objects such as {"id": 123}.

from corm import Entity, Field, KeyManager, KeyNested, Storage


class User(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)


class UserKeyManager(KeyManager):
    def get(self, data: dict[str, int]) -> int:
        return data["id"]

    def prepare_to_set(self, entity: Entity | None) -> dict[str, int] | None:
        if entity is None:
            return None
        assert isinstance(entity, User)
        return {"id": entity.id}


class Team(Entity):
    members: list[User] = KeyNested(
        User.id, origin="member_refs", key_manager=UserKeyManager()
    )


storage = Storage()
amina = User({"id": 123}, storage)
lee = User({"id": 456}, storage)
team = Team({"member_refs": [{"id": 123}]}, storage)

assert team.members == [amina]
assert team.dict() == {"member_refs": [{"id": 123}]}

team.members = [amina, lee]

assert team.members == [amina, lee]
assert team.dict() == {"member_refs": [{"id": 123}, {"id": 456}]}

docs.title: Nested relationships
docs.text:
Nested() and Relationship() infer the related entity type and whether the field holds one entity or a list. Use Address for a single entity and list[Address] for a list. Quoted forward references such as "Address" and list["Address"] are resolved through the entity registry when needed. Optional annotations such as Address | None and Optional[list[Address]] infer the same type and cardinality as their non-optional forms.

You can still pass entity_type= and many= explicitly. Each explicit argument overrides the corresponding inference.

docs.title: Simple relationship
docs.text:
Nested wraps an embedded dictionary as an entity, so a user can access the address fields through user.address.

from corm import Entity, Nested, Storage


class Address(Entity):
    street: str
    number: int


class User(Entity):
    name: str
    address: Address = Nested()


storage = Storage()
john = User(
    data={
        "name": "John",
        "address": {
            "street": "First",
            "number": 1,
        },
    },
    storage=storage,
)

assert john.address.street == "First"
assert john.address.number == 1

docs.title: Bidirectional relationships
docs.text:
Set back_populates on the Nested field to name the Relationship on the related entity. Each pair has its own links, so fields such as Order.billing and Order.shipping can both point to Address and have separate reverse fields.

The reverse field's annotation or many= setting controls whether it returns one owner or a list of owners. corm resolves the pair when the first owning entity is created, which allows forward references. Target subclasses can use the pair by inheriting its Relationship.

When a redefined owner class takes over a back_populates pair, instances of the superseded class are stale and their behavior is undefined.

from corm import Entity, Nested, Relationship, Storage


class Address(Entity):
    street: str
    number: int
    user: "User | None" = Relationship()


class User(Entity):
    name: str
    address: Address | None = Nested(back_populates="user")


storage = Storage()
john = User(
    data={
        "name": "John",
        "address": {
            "street": "First",
            "number": 1,
        },
    },
    storage=storage,
)

assert john.address is not None
assert john.address.user == john

docs.title: Self-nested
docs.text:
A pair can connect two fields on the same entity class. Appending a child to another parent's list or assigning its parent moves it from its old parent.

from corm import Entity, Nested, Relationship, Storage


class Item(Entity):
    id: int
    items: list["Item"] = Nested(back_populates="parent", default=list)
    parent: "Item | None" = Relationship()


storage = Storage()
item1 = Item({"id": 1, "items": [{"id": 2}, {"id": 3}]}, storage)
item2, item3 = item1.items

assert item1.id == 1
assert item1.parent is None

assert item2.id == 2
assert item2.parent == item1
assert item2.items == []

assert item3.id == 3
assert item3.parent == item1
assert item3.items == []

item3.items.append(item2)
assert item2.parent is item3
assert item1.items == [item3]

item2.parent = item1
assert item1.items == [item3, item2]
assert item3.items == []

docs.title: Change relationships between entities
docs.text:
You can write through either field. Assign a new owner to a single Relationship to move the related entity, or assign None to unlink it. If the new owner holds a single value, the move replaces that value and clears the displaced entity's reverse link.

from corm import Entity, Nested, Relationship, Storage


class Address(Entity):
    street: str
    user: "User | None" = Relationship()


class User(Entity):
    id: int
    address: Address | None = Nested(back_populates="user")


storage = Storage()
john = User(
    data={
        "id": 1,
        "name": "John",
        "description": "john smith",
        "address": {
            "street": "kirova",
        },
    },
    storage=storage,
)

old_address = john.address

assert old_address is not None
assert old_address.user is john

address = Address(data={"street": "lenina"}, storage=storage)
john.address = address

assert old_address.user is None
assert address.user is john
assert john.address is address

jane = User({"id": 2, "address": {"street": "First"}}, storage)
displaced = jane.address
assert displaced is not None
address.user = jane

assert john.address is None
assert jane.address is address
assert address.user is jane
assert displaced.user is None

address.user = None
assert jane.address is None
assert address.user is None

On either side, a list can be edited in place or replaced. Appending or removing an owner through a reverse list updates that owner's field.

from corm import Entity, Nested, Relationship, Storage


class Address(Entity):
    street: str
    users: list["User"] = Relationship()


class User(Entity):
    id: int
    addresses: list[Address] = Nested(back_populates="users", default=list)


storage = Storage()
john = User(
    data={
        "id": 1,
        "name": "John",
        "description": "john smith",
        "addresses": [
            {
                "street": "kirova 1",
            },
            {
                "street": "kirova 2",
            },
        ],
    },
    storage=storage,
)

old_address1, old_address2 = john.addresses

# you can change existing list
john.addresses.remove(old_address1)

assert old_address1.users == []
assert old_address2.users == [john]

john.addresses.clear()

assert old_address1.users == []
assert old_address2.users == []
assert john.addresses == []

new_address1 = Address(data={"street": "lenina 1"}, storage=storage)
new_address2 = Address(data={"street": "lenina 2"}, storage=storage)

john.addresses.append(new_address1)

assert new_address1.users == [john]
assert john.addresses == [new_address1]

john.addresses.extend([new_address2])

assert new_address2.users == [john]
assert john.addresses == [new_address1, new_address2]

# or completely replace it
john.addresses = [old_address1]

assert new_address1.users == []
assert new_address2.users == []
assert old_address1.users == [john]

jane = User({"id": 2}, storage)
old_address1.users.append(jane)
assert jane.addresses == [old_address1]

old_address1.users.remove(john)
assert john.addresses == []

old_address1.users = [john]
assert jane.addresses == []
assert john.addresses == [old_address1]

The older back_relation parameter still works and emits a DeprecationWarning. To migrate, replace it with back_populates="reverse_field_name".

docs.title: Manually related entities
docs.text:
A standalone Relationship uses relation_type to read and write links managed directly by Storage. This example links a user to an address and then removes the link.

from corm import Entity, Relationship, RelationType, Storage

storage = Storage()


class Address(Entity):
    street: str
    number: int


class User(Entity):
    name: str
    address: Address | None = Relationship(relation_type=RelationType.PARENT)


address = Address({"street": "First", "number": 1}, storage)
john = User({"name": "John"}, storage)

storage.make_relation(
    from_=john,
    to_=address,
    relation_type=RelationType.PARENT,
)

assert john.address == address

storage.remove_relation(
    from_=john,
    to_=address,
    relation_type=RelationType.PARENT,
)

assert john.address is None

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Storage is an in-memory identity map and relation index. Create one Storage() per loaded document and share it among that document's entities. Nested entities inherit their owner's storage. The storage holds strong references to indexed entities and relation endpoints, so they can live as long as the storage does, even after you drop your own references to them.

docs.title: Primary keys
docs.text:
Mark a field with Field(pk=True) to register each entity by that field and its value. storage.get(User.id, 1) returns the registered instance, or None if the key is absent. A key must be hashable. corm indexes each primary-key field separately, so two different fields can use the same key.

Creating another entity with the same key on the same field raises DuplicateKeyError. Assigning a new key through an entity attribute moves the index entry. A conflicting assignment raises the same error and leaves the original key and index entry in place.

docs.title: Dangling key references
docs.text:
A KeyNested field can be loaded before its target. Each read looks up the stored key in the same storage. If the key is missing, reading the field raises EntityNotFoundError with the default required=True. Set required=False to return None for an unresolved single reference or skip unresolved keys in a list. The stored keys remain in the data.

Changing the target's primary key leaves existing references at their stored values. The example shows the old reference becoming unresolved and a reference waiting for the new key resolving to the same user.

from corm import Entity, Field, KeyNested, Relationship, Storage


class User(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)
    addresses: list["Address"] = Relationship()


class Address(Entity):
    user: User | None = KeyNested(
        User.id, origin="user_id", back_populates="addresses", required=False
    )


storage = Storage()
old_address = Address({"user_id": 1}, storage)
new_address = Address({"user_id": 5}, storage)
user = User({"id": 1}, storage)
assert old_address.user is user
assert new_address.user is None

user.id = 5

assert storage.get(User.id, 1) is None
assert storage.get(User.id, 5) is user
assert old_address.user is None
assert old_address.dict() == {"user_id": 1}
assert new_address.user is user
assert user.addresses == [new_address]

docs.title: Manual relations
docs.text:
Use make_relation(from_=source, to_=target, relation_type=kind) to add a directed link for a standalone Relationship with a matching relation_type. Use remove_relation with the same arguments to unlink it. Adding an existing link or removing a missing one raises RelationError. For paired Nested and KeyNested fields, assign or edit the relation attributes to update the payload and index together.

get_related_entities() returns a new list in relation order. Editing that list leaves the storage index unchanged.

This example adds and removes a manual link from a user to an address.

from corm import Entity, Relationship, RelationType, Storage

storage = Storage()


class Address(Entity):
    street: str
    number: int


class User(Entity):
    name: str
    address: Address | None = Relationship(relation_type=RelationType.PARENT)


address = Address({"street": "First", "number": 1}, storage)
john = User({"name": "John"}, storage)

storage.make_relation(
    from_=john,
    to_=address,
    relation_type=RelationType.PARENT,
)

assert john.address == address

storage.remove_relation(
    from_=john,
    to_=address,
    relation_type=RelationType.PARENT,
)

assert john.address is None
